Pick one written security procedure and ask someone to explain how it works today.

A useful Saturday check is the gap between the document and the actual routine. Does the procedure name a system you no longer use? Does it send approvals to a role that changed? Are people following a newer process that never made it into the document?

We at Cloud2e provide CMMC preparation services that include System Security Plan, POA&M, and policy documentation support. That work connects written descriptions with the environment and activities they are meant to explain.

Keep the review small. Compare one procedure with the responsible team's current instructions, record discrepancies, and route updates through your approval process. Include a review date so the next person knows when it was checked.

The intended benefit is documentation people can use and maintain as operations change.

posts.company:
A technology change can leave a documentation change unfinished.

An organization may replace a tool, adjust an approval route, or move a service while its written procedures continue describing the previous arrangement. Over time, that makes it harder to explain how work is actually performed.

Cloud2e's CMMC preparation services include System Security Plan, POA&M, and policy documentation support alongside gap assessment and remediation.

One practical improvement is to add a documentation check to your normal change review. Ask which system descriptions, procedures, diagrams, or supporting records the change affects. Assign the update and capture its approval with the change record.

When no update is needed, record that decision too. The purpose is to make the review visible and repeatable rather than depend on someone remembering later.

This helps technical teams and business stakeholders work from a consistent description of the environment.
